challenge_record.target: Filesystem-based routing as the central organizing principle
challenge_record.challenge: If filesystem routing is removed and replaced with an explicit route registry, what invariants break? The answer: none that are architectural. Routing still works, middleware still applies, versioning still works. What is lost is ceremony reduction and the 'structure = architecture' mental model — but those are developer-experience benefits, not correctness guarantees. The system's runtime behavior is identical whether routes are declared in files or in an Express router.
evidence: package.json already has lint:boundaries — explicit boundary enforcement, suggesting implicit filesystem boundaries need explicit reinforcement
api/[...notfound].ts documents dynamic-route precedence as 'lowest' — implicit ordering is a known gotcha that explicit routing would make visible
Maintainer mental model says 'the files tell the story' but the same repo has ARCHITECTURE.md and docs/architecture.mdx — the story is already told twice, filesystem is not the sole narrative
challenge_record.model_delta: Filesystem routing is an ergonomic optimization, not an architectural invariant. The architecture's organizing principle is 'convention-enforced-by-CI', where the filesystem is one convention among many (alongside lint scripts, underscore prefix, and boundary checks). Downgrade from 'central organizing principle' to 'developer-ergonomic routing mechanism validated by CI'.

challenge_record.target: Token-overlap scoring is deliberately not NLU for deterministic agent routing
challenge_record.challenge: What if the opposite were true — that NLU-based routing would be strictly better? Then we would expect to see: (a) evidence that token-overlap failures (semantic paraphrasing producing wrong tool routing) are caught and logged, (b) fallback mechanisms when token-overlap confidence is low, (c) telemetry showing token-overlap accuracy vs. a ground-truth routing table. None of these exist in the evidence. The claim 'deliberately not NLU' is asserted without showing that the deterministic tradeoff was empirically measured against actual agent query traffic.
evidence: api/_agent-tool-suggest.ts: 'Deliberately not NLU' — no accuracy measurement, no fallback path, no telemetry cited
Repository Model: A2A and NLWeb are listed as '双向' (bidirectional) with API Gateway — agents send queries and expect correct routing, but there's no evidence of routing accuracy being monitored
ARCHITECTURE.md does not mention tool-routing accuracy as an SLO
tension section already flags 'Agent-consumable API vs human-facing SPA' as a tension — token-overlap sits at the intersection and has no quality gate
challenge_record.model_delta: Token-overlap routing is a pragmatic starting point, not a deliberate architectural tradeoff. The decision is better characterized as 'Default to simplest working solution; upgrade to NLU when token-overlap failures reach a measured threshold.' Add routing accuracy telemetry as a future requirement, not an afterthought.

challenge_record.target: No message queue or event bus between API Gateway and Backend Server
challenge_record.challenge: This omission holds only under the assumption that request-response freshness is always preferred over async decoupling. But the evidence contradicts this: the system has multi-region edge compute (decentralized pre-processing) AND a centralized Backend Server aggregating from dozens of external sources. Edge compute implies state that needs coordination; dozens of sources imply variable latency. The synchronous HTTP boundary between Gateway and Backend means a slow backend pipeline (waiting for a slow external source) blocks the entire API Gateway thread pool. The 'no queue' decision is not a deliberate tradeoff — it is an omission that will become a problem at the next scale increment.
evidence: Repository Model: Backend Server owns 'Observability & SLO tracking across 30+ domains' — 30+ external sources with heterogeneous latency profiles
Repository Model: Backend Server owns 'Multi-region deployment & edge compute' — edge implies partially processed state that needs to be reconciled with centralized aggregation
Repository Model: API Gateway → Backend Server is marked '单向' (unidirectional) synchronous — no backpressure mechanism, no circuit breaker documented

evolution.major_changes: 'Multi-region deployment & edge compute integration' — edge compute was added after the sync architecture was built, suggesting the sync boundary was not designed for edge coordination
challenge_record.model_delta: The no-queue omission is not a deliberate architectural decision but a scalability debt. The correct characterization is 'Synchronous Gateway-Backend boundary, designed when external source count and edge compute were not in the original scope. Queue/deferred-processing should be added when: (1) any single external source latency exceeds Gateway timeout, or (2) edge-compute reconciliation requires stateful handoff between regions.'

challenge_record.target: Compile-time enforcement via 8 separate JS/TS lint scripts is a well-designed contract boundary
challenge_record.challenge: The enforcer and the enforced share the same runtime (Node.js), the same language (JS/TS), and potentially the same bugs. A bug in enforce-sebuf-api-contract.mjs could silently accept invalid API contracts. A bug in the boundary lint script could miss a dependency violation. Unlike a type system (which is formally verified) or a separate process (which has different failure modes), these scripts are code checking code of the same kind — meta-circular validation. The question is not whether enforcement is valuable (it is), but whether 8 separate scripts is the right abstraction level vs. a single policy engine with composable rules.
evidence: architectural_tensions: 'Lint scripts (JavaScript/TypeScript) enforce contracts on other JavaScript/TypeScript code — the enforcer and the enforced share the same runtime and could share the same bugs'
package.json: 8 separate scripts — enforce-sebuf-api-contract, enforce-rate-limit-policies, enforce-premium-fetch, enforce-safe-html, enforce-intlify-slugs, docs-stats, boundary-lint, format check
Maintainer mental model: 'each script owns exactly one concern' — but there's no documented ordering, dependency graph, or shared utility layer among them
challenge_record.model_delta: The 8-script design is not wrong but is incomplete — it needs (a) a shared validation utility library to prevent duplicate logic across scripts, (b) a script-ordering policy (which scripts must pass before which others), and (c) a self-test suite for the enforcement scripts themselves (meta-validation). The tension 'same runtime, same bugs' is real and should be mitigated by making each script small enough to be trivially correct, not by accepting the risk.

challenge_record.target: Desktop Tauri origins validated in the same _api-key.js as standard web origins
challenge_record.challenge: This design puts two fundamentally different security models (web CORS with Origin header vs. non-web desktop with custom origins Tauri://, asset://) into a single middleware file with a single DESKTOP_ORIGIN_PATTERNS regex check. The conditions under which this breaks: (1) a browser-based attack that spoofs Origin to a Tauri pattern — any Tauri pattern that resembles a web origin (https://tauri.localhost) is browser-constructible; (2) adding a new desktop runtime (Electron, SwiftUI) would require modifying the same patterns array in the same file, widening the attack surface without architectural review; (3) the middleware has no way to distinguish a real Tauri WebView from a regular browser that happens to set Origin: tauri://localhost.
evidence: api/_api-key.js: DESKTOP_ORIGIN_PATTERNS includes /^https?:\/\/tauri\.localhost/ — this regex matches any HTTP/HTTPS origin with tauri.localhost, which any browser can set via document.domain or fetch with custom Origin header
architectural_tensions: 'Two security models sharing one middleware file' — this is already identified as a tension, not a resolved design
evolution.major_changes: 'Desktop runtime (Tauri) support: added DESKTOP_ORIGIN_PATTERNS' — desktop was added after the fact, not designed in; patterns were appended to existing code
challenge_record.model_delta: The DESKTOP_ORIGIN_PATTERNS check is insufficient as a standalone security boundary. The correct architecture requires: (a) desktop clients must present a proof-of-possession key (e.g., a desktop-only API key compiled into the Tauri binary, rotated at build time) in addition to the origin check; (b) the https://tauri.localhost pattern must be removed or restricted (it is browser-forgeable); (c) desktop auth flow should be a separate middleware module, not an if-branch in the web auth middleware.

challenge_record.target: No database/ORM layer — aggregation pipeline doesn't need persistent storage
challenge_record.chain_target: No database/ORM layer — aggregation pipeline doesn't need persistent storage
challenge_record.challenge: The claim 'World Monitor is an aggregation pipeline + API gateway, not a CRUD application' assumes data freshness is the only concern and persistence is not required. But the evidence shows: edge compute (which needs intermediate state), session tokens (which need server-side TTL management), multi-region deployment (which needs configuration synchronization), and 'Observability & SLO tracking across 30+ domains' (which implies metrics storage and historical comparison). Each of these independently suggests a need for persistent state. The 'no database' decision likely holds for the current implementation but will be violated incrementally: first a file-based cache for edge state, then SQLite for session management, then a time-series store for SLO tracking — each added ad-hoc rather than designed.
evidence: Repository Model: Backend Server owns 'Observability & SLO tracking across 30+ domains' — SLO tracking implies historical metrics, which implies storage, which is a database

Repository Model: API Middleware owns session tokens — session tokens with TTL/revocation (implied by 'session-token-based API key validation') require server-side state, which is a database or cache (Redis/memcached)
evolution.major_changes: 'Multi-region deployment & edge compute integration' — multi-region implies configuration distribution and state reconciliation, which strains a stateless architecture
intentional_omissions say 'no database' but the module responsibilities describe behavior that non-trivially implies storage
challenge_record.model_delta: The 'no database' claim is true only at the source code level (no SQL/ORM imports) but false at the architectural level (session state, SLO metrics, edge-compute state all require persistence). The correct characterization is 'no visible database — storage is implicit in middleware/server responsibilities and should be made explicit.' The architecture should document what state is stored, where, and with what durability guarantees — even if the answer is 'in-memory only, loss acceptable.'

challenge_record.target: SPA architecture for a real-time global intelligence dashboard
challenge_record.challenge: A real-time intelligence dashboard aggregating from dozens of external sources with multi-region edge compute implies a data-fetching topology that fights the SPA model. In a SPA, the client initiates all requests; in a real-time intelligence system, the server should push updates (WebSocket, SSE). The SPA trades true real-time push for simpler deployment (static files) and SEO (which the system doesn't need — it's a dashboard, not a content site). The tradeoff documentation says 'SEO and initial load latency' as downsides, but the bigger downside is missed: every 'real-time' update requires either polling from the SPA or a WebSocket connection — and WebSocket would require a different deployment topology (stateful server) than the static-SPA model supports. The current architecture has an implicit 'pull-model for real-time data' contradiction.
evidence: ARCHITECTURE.md: 'real-time global intelligence dashboard' — real-time implies push, SPA implies pull; these are contradictory without a WebSocket/SSE layer that the module list doesn't include
Repository Model modules: no WebSocket server, no SSE endpoint, no event-notification channel listed in public_api or plugin_points
Repository Model: Frontend SPA → API Gateway is '单向' (unidirectional) — SPA only pulls from Gateway, Gateway never pushes to SPA

tradeoffs: 'SPA architecture gives rich real-time dashboard experience at the cost of SEO and initial load latency' — misses the fundamental contradiction: without push, the dashboard can only be 'near-real-time' at poll interval granularity
challenge_record.model_delta: The SPA architecture is not designed for real-time push — it is a polling-based near-real-time dashboard. The architecture should be characterized as 'Poll-based near-real-time dashboard with SPA frontend; WebSocket/SSE push is a planned capability (or deliberate omission) that must be documented.' The term 'real-time' should be qualified to 'near-real-time with configurable poll interval.'
